title: Goldman Sachs CEO: We Don't Support Trump Travel Order
description: Jan.30 -- In a sharply worded message to staff, Goldman Sachs CEO Lloyd Blankfein broke with the Trump administration over its controversial attempt to crack down on immigration. Bloomberg's Dakin Campbell reports on "Bloomberg Markets."

asr.full_text: Dakin many CEOs have taken this action they want their employees know that if they have heritage in other countries or you know if they want to travel to other countries or have several passports that they're still welcome to work there yes it's true it the notable thing about Lloyd Blankfein's voicemail was sort of how directly he said that he and the firm Goldman Sachs didn't support the policy. As I was reading the news over the weekend and saw the memos that CEOs sent out, it was pretty notable that many of them said we're in favor of immigration, we're in favor of the contributions that immigrants have given to our corporation. But they didn't really take on the Trump administration directly or comment on the policy directly. And Lloyd's voicemail, he had said very clearly, this is a policy we do not support. And so that was pretty interesting. Help us understand the cultural import of this within the financial sector. SO THAT WAS PRETTY INTERESTING. HELP US UNDERSTAND THE CULTURAL IMPORT OF THIS WITHIN THE FINANCIAL SECTOR. OVER THE WEEKEND, THERE WAS A STREAM OF MEMORANDUM FROM SILICON VALLEY EXECUTIVES FIRST OF ALL. BANKING SEEMED TO GET IN ON THIS LATE IN THE GAME. WITH GOLDMAN IN SPECIFIC, WHY IS IT SO IMPORTANT? IT'S A GOOD QUESTION. AND I'M NOT PRIVY TO LOUIS'S WHAT HE WAS THINKING WHEN HE DID THIS. BUT ONE THING WITH THE TECH CEOS, THEY HAVE MANY EMPLOYEES WHO ARE AFFECTED. I THINK IN GOOGLE'S CASE A COUPLE OF THEM WERE ACTUALLY CAUGHT IN THE AIRPORTS, SO THEY WERE SORT OF DRIVEN TO RESPOND A LITTLE QUICKER THAN WALL STREET WAS. BUT IN THE LAST FEW YEARS WALL STREET HAS BEEN COMPETING VERY CLOSELY WITH TECHNOLOGY AND OTHER SECTORS BUT REALLY WITH than Wall Street was. But in the last few years, Wall Street has been competing very closely with technology and other sectors, but really with Silicon Valley, over talent for people. And so one aspect of this is sort of positioning yourself as, hey, this is not something we're going to stand for. Deakin, what other bank executives, financial services executives are talking about this as it relates to Brexit too, because it feels like suddenly there's no home for banks or financial services anymore. It's true. J.P. Morgan's operating committee put a memo out over the weekend and they said essentially that while they're in support of, you know, defending the country and safety, they thought immigration and diversity was really important. So obviously Jamie Dimon is one of the people that sits on that operating committee. He's been outspoken in favor of immigration in the past. Wells Fargo and Morgan Stanley had memos out that essentially said we're looking at how this affects our employees. They didn't take on the policy directly. Citigroup and Bank of America so far have declined to comment entirely. STONE STONEFIELD, Citi Group President and Bank of America Senior Senior Officer at Citigroup Steve Schwartzman as well. DAVID LAPIN, Citi Group Administrator and Bank of America Senior Officer at Citigroup And Steve Schwartzman as well. STONEFIELD, Citi Group Vice President and Bank of America Senior Officer at Citigroup So, it's this continuum of people who feel comfortable for whatever reason to sort of take on the policy all the way to CEOs and management teams who think that, you know, their duty to get out of the way, to get out of AND A CONTINUUM OF PEOPLE WHO FEEL COMFORTABLE, FOR WHATEVER REASON, TO SORT OF TAKE ON THE POLICY ALL THE WAY TO CEOs AND MANAGEMENT TEAMS WHO THINK, YOU KNOW, THAT THIS IS THEIR DUTY OR IT'S SAFEST TO JUST STAY OUT OF IT. YOU'VE READ THESE. IS THE AUDIENCE FOR THESE MEMOS REALLY THE EMPLOYEES THEMSELVES? WERE THESE GEARED TOWARD THE PUBLIC AND GEARED TOWARD CUSTOMERS AS WELL? GOOD QUESTION. I THINK PROBABLY BOTH. BUT I THINK WITH MOST CORPORATE MEMOS, THESE DAYS THEY'RE GEARED TOWARDS THE PUBLIC, AND PUBLIC CONSUMPTION. Good question. I think probably both, but I think with most corporate memos these days, they're geared towards the public and public consumption. So but I do think that if it didn't affect employees, these CEOs wouldn't feel the need to sort of, you know, take on the administration. Right. Trump has been, YOU KNOW, VERY – HE HAS SHOWN THAT HE'S WILLING TO TAKE ON COMPANIES THAT DON'T – THAT HE DOESN'T AGREE WITH OR THAT DON'T AGREE WITH HIM. SO I DON'T THINK THE DECISION IS MADE LIGHTLY TO SORT OF GO OUT AGAINST A POLICY OF HIS, YOU KNOW. I THINK THE CALCULUS HAS TO INCLUDE EMPLOYEES. I DON'T THINK THERE ARE THEN ANY IN SUPPORT OF THE POLICY HAVE THERE? NOT THAT I – Not a lot I�VE SEEN, YES.

annotation.contextual_rationale: This video is non-scam content because it presents a Bloomberg news interview and report about Goldman Sachs's response to an immigration-related travel policy. The discussion analyzes corporate memos, employee concerns, and whether financial firms publicly opposed the policy, placing it in a political and business-news context rather than a financial scheme. The frames and supplied text identify the segment and subject, although they do not independently verify the underlying policy statements.
